title: Praying alone
hook: without ten people some parts are skipped, but the prayer still counts

segments.voice: Yesterday, sefirat ha'omer, the omer counted up at nightfall. Your line was count by night. Today, what happens when you're the only one in the room.

A hospital waiting room at six in the morning. A soldier on a base far from any synagogue. A student in a dorm who just isn't going to make it to services. A grandmother at her kitchen window before anyone else is up. For weeks, this path has walked through the service as a congregation says it: the leader, the answers, the ten. But on any given morning, some Jews pray with a congregation, and some pray by themselves. What happens to the prayer then?
screen: `A HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `A KITCHEN WINDOW.` → `ONE PERSON, ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, what's missing. Jewish law says certain parts are matters of holiness, said only with a minyan of ten. Without ten, you leave out Barchu, the call to prayer. The Kedushah, the holy, holy, holy said standing together. The leader's repetition of the Amidah. The Torah reading. And the Kaddish, met earlier on this path. Those are real losses, and the rabbis didn't pretend otherwise. The Talmud says a prayer said with the community is especially welcome, and encourages someone alone to pray at the same time the congregation does, joined in time if not in place. But here's the other half. The heart of the service, the Shema and the Amidah, is complete when you say it alone. It counts. Fully. And the model for the silent Amidah is one woman praying by herself: Hannah, in the book of Samuel, at the sanctuary in Shiloh, with no one praying alongside her. In the old Jewish translation: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The priest who saw her thought she was drunk. The Talmud draws lessons for all prayer from that one scene: pray with intention, move your lips, keep your voice quiet. So the silent Amidah, said by a whole congregation standing together, is built on a woman praying alone. At its quietest moment, the congregation is copying her.
screen: `WITHOUT TEN: NO BARCHU, NO KEDUSHAH.` · `PRAY WHEN THE CONGREGATION PRAYS.` · `THE HEART OF IT IS COMPLETE.` · `HANNAH, ALONE AT SHILOH.` · then, large: `ALONE STILL COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Sit alone with intention, praying if prayer is yours, with no one to follow and no one to answer you. Do what Hannah did: let your lips move, keep your voice too low to hear, and say something real, a thanks, a worry, a hope, and if you like, picture the others in kitchens and waiting rooms doing the same right now.
Praying alone. Without ten, some parts drop away, but the Shema and the Amidah are whole, and the silent prayer is modeled on Hannah.
Your line: alone still counts. The heart of it is whole, even with no one else there. Day six hundred thirteen, done.

howItsDone: Someone praying without a minyan says the Shema, its blessings and the Amidah in full, and leaves out Barchu, Kedushah, the repetition of the Amidah, the Torah reading and the Kaddish; many try to pray at the same time as their community's service.

chat.says: If I can't get to synagogue, does praying by myself even count?
options: Yes; the Shema and Amidah are complete alone, though some parts need ten.
Only if you can hear ten other people praying somewhere nearby.
No; without ten, Jewish law says the whole service is skipped.
